faq.a: Autoregulation can keep GFR stable only down to MAP ≈ 80 mmHg; below that afferent dilation is insufficient, so flow and filtration drop together.
faq.q: Why does renal blood flow fall before GFR in shock?

faq.a: It is mainly for hepatorenal syndrome; in pure hypovolaemia it may worsen splanchnic ischemia, so reserve for portal‑hypertension‑related cases.
faq.q: Can terlipressin be used in patients without liver disease?

faq.a: A tense, fluid‑filled abdomen with reduced breath sounds and a high bladder pressure (>20 cm H₂O) indicates ascites‑related pressure.
faq.q: What bedside sign suggests intra‑abdominal pressure is impairing RBF?

exam: A 28‑year‑old with severe malaria presents with oliguria and MAP 70 mmHg. – Explain the pathophysiology of reduced RBF and immediate management steps.
How does tubuloglomerular feedback protect GFR when MAP falls to 85 mmHg? – Describe the macula densa mechanism.
A patient on chronic NSAIDs develops AKI; differentiate pre‑renal from intrinsic causes using urine findings. – List expected sediment and fractional excretion of Na.
In a child with sickle cell disease and vaso‑occlusive crisis, why might renal blood flow be paradoxically increased? – Discuss hyperfiltration and its risks.
Explain why norepinephrine is preferred over dopamine in septic shock affecting renal perfusion. – Include receptor actions and side‑effect profile.
A patient with schistosomiasis‑related portal hypertension has rising creatinine; what pharmacologic agents improve RBF and why? – Mention terlipressin, midodrine, octreotide.
When is renal ultrasound essential in evaluating low urine output in a low‑resource setting? – Indicate findings that change management.
Describe the clinical consequences of prolonged MAP < 80 mmHg on renal tubular cells. – Link ischemia to acute tubular necrosis.
ai.title: Renal Blood Flow and Autoregulation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Renal blood flow (RBF) is tightly regulated by myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback to keep GFR stable across a range of blood pressures. In low‑resource settings, recognising pre‑renal failure and the impact of volume status, sepsis, and portal hypertension is crucial.

b: Myogenic response: arteriolar smooth muscle contracts when pressure rises, dilates when pressure falls.
Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF): macula densa senses NaCl delivery and adjusts afferent tone.
sections.p: Renal blood flow is the volume of plasma delivered to the kidneys per minute (≈1 L/min in adults). Autoregulation keeps GFR constant when mean arterial pressure (MAP) is 80‑180 mmHg.

b: Stage 1: ↑Scr 1.5‑1.9× baseline or urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6‑12 h.
Stage 2: ↑Scr 2‑2.9× baseline or urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 h.
Stage 3: ↑Scr ≥3× baseline or urine <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h.
sections.p: RBF itself is not staged, but its failure is graded by the resulting acute kidney injury (AKI) using KDIGO criteria based on creatinine rise and urine output.

b: Hypovolaemia (diarrhoea, vomiting, malaria, severe burns).
Septic shock (bacterial, malaria, typhoid, TB meningitis).
Cardiac failure (rheumatic heart disease, peripartum cardiomyopathy).
Portal hypertension with splanchnic vasodilation (schistosomiasis, advanced hepatitis B).
Nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, herbal remedies).
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals the most common precipitants of reduced RBF are volume depletion and sepsis; tropical infections add specific risks.

b: Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h.
Dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, low MAP.
Peripheral edema or ascites in chronic liver disease.
sections.p: Patients present with oliguria, rising creatinine, and signs of systemic hypoperfusion; in portal hypertension they may have ascites‑related intra‑abdominal pressure worsening RBF.

t.b: Is systemic perfusion adequate? MAP < 80 mmHg suggests autoregulatory failure.
What is renal function? Rising values confirm AKI.
Is the kidney excreting enough fluid? Quantifies oliguria.
Is there renal cortical thickness loss or hydronephrosis? Helps rule out obstructive causes.
Are there disturbances from reduced perfusion? Guides fluid management.

b: Persistent MAP < 65 mmHg despite fluids.
Anuria >12 h.
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.2).
Pulmonary oedema from fluid overload in cardiac failure.
sections.p: Uncorrected low RBF quickly leads to irreversible tubular injury and systemic complications.

b: Fluid resuscitation: isotonic crystalloids 20‑30 mL/kg bolus; repeat if MAP remains <80 mmHg.
Vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) when fluids insufficient; avoid dopamine due to tachyarrhythmia risk.
Treat infection promptly with appropriate antibiotics; consider antimalarials or anti‑TB drugs where indicated.
If portal hypertension, terlipressin or midodrine + octreotide can raise systemic resistance and improve RBF.
Stop nephrotoxic drugs and herbal preparations.
sections.p: Restore perfusion, treat the underlying cause, and avoid further nephrotoxicity.

b: Re‑measure creatinine at 48 h and 7 days.
Educate on safe use of NSAIDs and traditional medicines.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and malaria prophylaxis for at‑risk patients.
sections.p: Monitor urine output, creatinine, and MAP daily; educate patients on hydration and avoidance of nephrotoxins.

b: ATN: intrinsic injury, often after prolonged ischemia; urine sediment shows granular casts.
Post‑renal: obstruction; bladder distension or hydronephrosis on ultrasound.
sections.p: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and post‑renal obstruction can both cause oliguria but have different pathophysiology.

b: Rely on trends, not a single value.
Combine clinical assessment with bedside ultrasound when labs are limited.
sections.p: Serum creatinine may be normal early in hypovolaemia because of reduced production; urine output may be low from dehydration rather than intrinsic kidney damage.

whenToSeekHelp: MAP remains <65 mmHg after 2 fluid boluses
